title: Man. Post. Cap. I: Garissoles on Chamier duplex; Placeus rejects imputed/inherent split
pass_a_gloss: GARISSOLES. Chamier manifestly distinguishes two things in Original Sin: that it is the penalty of the first sin, and that it is an internal vice inhering in us. But the former did not come into controversy with Pighius and others whom he refutes in that book; therefore he does not urge that consideration in this place. But it was asked only whether original sin had the true character of vice and corruption. Chamier affirms and proves; and considering original sin now as it is vice, not without desert he constitutes its nature in those three. PLACEUS. Whither that distinction looks, I know not. For who ever said original sin is twofold: one, the penalty of the first actual sin, the other, inherent vice; or that there are two parts of original sin: one the penalty of the first sin, the other an internal sin inhering in us? But those who teach the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin say either that original sin is twofold—one imputed, the other inherent—or that there are two parts of original sin; the primary and chief the imputed actual sin of Adam, the less chief hereditary corruption. If Chamier was of that opinion, how did he assert that in those three which he recounted the whole nature of original sin is contained? How did he add, Therefore when these are demonstrated nothing will be left remaining? For he would have omitted the chief part of original sin. Add that if the Pelagian heresy was partly situated in the denial of that imputation, as D. Garissoles wished, it behooved Catholics to demonstrate that imputation first of all, especially since it had been openly denied by Stapleton and some other Papists. But of Chamier, if there will be need, it will be disputed elsewhere.
pass_b_english: GARISSOLES. Chamier clearly divides two things in original sin: that it is the penalty of the first sin, and that it is an inward vice inhering in us. The first was not in dispute with Pighius and the others he answers in that book, so he does not press it here. The only question was whether original sin has the true character of vice and corruption. Chamier affirms and proves it; and taking original sin as vice, he rightly sets its nature in those three heads. PLACEUS. I do not see what that distinction is for. Who ever called original sin twofold—one the penalty of the first actual sin, the other inherent vice—or made two parts of it, penalty and inward sin? Those who teach immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin do say either that original sin is twofold (imputed and inherent) or that it has two parts—the chief being Adam's imputed actual sin, the lesser hereditary corruption. If Chamier held that, how could he say those three heads contain the whole nature of original sin, or add that once they are proved nothing remains? He would have left out the chief part. And if Pelagian heresy partly lay in denying that imputation, as Garissoles claims, Catholics ought to have proved the imputation first of all, especially since Stapleton and some other Papists openly denied it. Of Chamier, if need be, elsewhere.
source_text: GARISSOLIUS. Chamierus duo in Peccato originali manifeste distinguit, quod poena est peccati primi, et quod vitium est internum in nobis haerens. Sed prius non veniebat in controversiam cum Pighio, et aliis quos eo libro refutat; itaque eam considerationem non urget hoc loco. Sed quaerebatur tantum, an peccatum originale veram haberet rationem vitii et corruptionis. Affirmat Chamierus, et probat; Et peccatum originale considerans jam, qua vitium est, haud immerito ejus naturam in illis tribus constituit. PLACEUS. Quorsum spectet ista distinctio, nescio? Quis enim unquam peccatum originale dixit esse duplex: unum, poenam peccati primi actualis, alterum, vitium inhaerens; aut duas esse peccati originalis partes: unam poenam peccati primi, alteram peccatum internum in nobis haerens? Sed qui imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis immediatam docent, illi, vel duplex esse dicunt peccatum originale: unum imputatum, alterum inhaerens; vel duas peccati originalis partes; primariam et praecipuam peccatum actuale Adami imputatum, minus praecipuam corruptionem haereditariam. In qua opinione si fuit Chamierus, quomodo in illis tribus, quae commemoravit, universam peccati originalis naturam contineri asseruit? Quomodo addidit; Itaque iis demonstratis nihil erit reliqui factum? Omississet enim praecipuam peccati originalis partem. Adde quod si haeresis Pelagiana in imputationis illius negatione pars sita fuit, ut voluit D. Garissolius, decuit Catholicos eam imputationem inprimis demonstrare, praesertim cum a Stapletono, aliisque nonnullis Pontificiis, aperte negata fuisset. Sed de Chamiero, si opus erit, alibi disputabitur.
